about: Range of motion of each joint (degrees, active, healthy adult), which way it bends, and what tennis asks of it. The game must never draw a joint outside 'range'. 'tennis' gives the angles elite players actually reach in strokes. Owner: Biomechanics Coach.

conventions.zero: Anatomical position: standing straight, arms at the sides, palms forward. 0 = that position.
conventions.flexion: Bending the joint (elbow, knee: closing the angle). Knee and elbow flexion = 180 − the inner angle between the two bones.
conventions.seen2D: Angles measured from video are the angle seen in the picture. A bend that points toward or away from the camera looks smaller (or larger) than it is, so 2D numbers are checks, not limits.
conventions.sides: left/right are the player's own. A left-hander mirrors a right-hander: swap left and right, nothing else.

sources.AAOS: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Joint Motion: Method of Measuring and Recording (1965); the same normal values are tabled in Norkin & White, Measurement of Joint Motion: A Guide to Goniometry, 5th ed. (F.A. Davis, 2016).
sources.Elliott2003: Elliott B, Fleisig G, Nicholls R, Escamilla R. Technique effects on upper limb loading in the tennis serve. J Sci Med Sport 2003;6(1):76–87 (shoulder external rotation in the serve ≈ 170°).
sources.Kovacs2011: Kovacs M, Ellenbecker T. An 8-stage model for evaluating the tennis serve. Sports Health 2011;3(6):504–513.
sources.Ellenbecker: Ellenbecker TS et al. Glenohumeral rotation range of motion in elite tennis players (e.g. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 1996;24(6):336–341; Am J Sports Med 2002): the playing shoulder gains external and loses internal rotation, about the same total arc.
sources.measured: datasets/anatomy/uso/measurements.json (Alcaraz, US Open, real time, camera behind him) and the compilation serves (slow motion; angles only).

neck.what: Cervical spine: where the head looks.
neck.bends: Chin to chest (flexion), head back (extension); turns either way.
neck.tennis: Head stays up and still through contact (eyes on the contact point) and only then follows the ball; at a serve's contact the head is tilted back ~30–45° looking up.

trunk.bends: Forward a lot, backward a little; rotates up to 45° each way on top of the hips (the hips add their own rotation).
trunk.tennis: Serve: shoulder-over-shoulder side bend (racket shoulder low at the loading, high at contact). Measured: trunk leans 10° at the toss, 11° at the deepest knee bend and ~18° at contact (picture plane, Alcaraz). Return stance: chest tipped forward over the knees.

shoulder.what: Glenohumeral joint plus the shoulder blade: the most mobile joint in the body.
shoulder.bends: Every direction. Arm up in front (flexion) or out to the side (abduction) to vertical; 60° backward. A shoulder can't put the upper arm behind the back across the spine: an arm that crosses the body's middle passes in front of the chest.
shoulder.tennis: Serve cocking: the racket arm twists back to ~170° of external rotation (that number includes the shoulder blade and the trunk arching back; Elliott 2003), then whips forward into internal rotation. Playing shoulder of tour players: ~+10° external, ~−10° internal rotation vs the other arm (Ellenbecker). Measured at contact: upper arm 14° from vertical (Alcaraz), toss arm within 7° of vertical at its highest.

elbow.bends: One way only: the forearm folds toward the biceps. Never backward beyond a few degrees of hyperextension; never sideways.
elbow.tennis: Serve: ~90–130° bent at the loading (measured racket elbow 127° at the deepest knee bend), nearly straight at contact (measured 13°; compilation of 10 pros: 3–15°). Forearm pronates hard through contact. A tucked toss arm still stops at ~145–150°.

wrist.bends: Palm toward the forearm (flexion), back of the hand toward the forearm (extension), a little side to side.
wrist.tennis: Forehand: laid back (extended ~40–60°) before contact, flexing toward neutral through it. Serve: extended during the racket drop, snapping toward flexion and ulnar deviation at contact.

hip.what: Ball and socket between pelvis and thigh.
hip.bends: Thigh forward and up (flexion), a little backward (extension), out to the side (abduction).
hip.tennis: Wide stances (return, split-step landing, slides) use abduction; open-stance forehands load the outside hip in flexion + internal rotation.

knee.bends: One way only: the shin folds behind the thigh, the knee points forward. Never backward. The knee points over the toes (slightly outward in a wide stance), never inward.
knee.tennis: Serve loading (measured, Alcaraz, side-on so it reads well from behind): front knee 49°, back knee 72°; compilation pros 31–58° front. Landing: front knee ~17°, back leg kicked up behind (~100°). Return stance: ~45–70°.

ankle.bends: Toes up (dorsiflexion), toes down (plantarflexion). The heel lifts in every push-off and split-step landing; deep squats need the full 20° of dorsiflexion.
ankle.tennis: Ready and return stances stand on the balls of the feet (heels light). Serve: both ankles plantarflex fully at take-off.

bodyProportions.about: Joint heights and segment lengths as fractions of standing height H, to scale to each pro's heightM.
bodyProportions.source: Drillis R, Contini R. Body Segment Parameters. Tech. Rep. 1166-03, New York University, 1966 (tabled in Winter DA, Biomechanics and Motor Control of Human Movement, 4th ed., Wiley 2009).
